entry.title: Bundle format
entry.content:
tik-evidence-bundle version 1 — the on-disk contract, the checks a reader runs, and the rules that govern change.

tik-evidence-bundle, version 1. A gzipped tar holding one ticket and everything its derivation needs.

tik bundle <id> --out evidence.tgz

bundle.edn                          the format name and version
actors                              the allowed-signers registry
pq-signers                          the ML-DSA-65 key registry, where the store keeps one
signatures.edn                      the signature policy, where the store sets one
roles.edn                           role membership, where the store keeps a register
delegation.edn                      the store's delegation policy, where it sets one
identity/<event-id>.edn             key bindings and delegations, as signed registry events
identity/<event-id>.sig.<fpr>       their authorship signatures
identity/keys/<kid>.pem             the issuer keys those bindings rest on
processes/by-hash/<hash>.edn        the definition the ticket pinned
processes/by-hash/<hash>.sig.<fpr>  its publication signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.edn      the append-only log
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.sig.<fpr>      authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqsig.<fpr>    post-quantum authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.witness.<fpr>  countersignatures over a head
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqwitness.<fpr>  ML-DSA-65 countersignatures sealing an ancestry
tickets/<uuid>/blobs/<hash>         attached artifacts, addressed by content
verify.sh                           a coreutils implementation of the checks
README.md                           what the recipient is holding

What a reader may assume

Every stored file’s name is the SHA-256 of its bytes, prefixed sha256-. Event and definition files carry a .edn suffix after the address; blobs are named by the bare address. sha256sum alone audits the archive.

Event bytes are exactly the hashed region. An event file holds the canonical serialization without its :event/id, because the filename is the id. Re-emitting a parsed event reproduces the file byte for byte.

Signatures are detached siblings. <id>.sig.<fingerprint> covers the event’s stored bytes under the tik-event namespace; <id>.witness.<fpr> covers a head under tik-witness; a definition’s .sig.<fpr> uses tik-process. Each verifies with ssh-keygen -Y verify against actors. <id>.pqsig.<fpr> is the raw FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 signature over the bytes tik-event-v1, a NUL byte, then the event’s stored bytes, by the pq-signers key whose DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo hashes (SHA-256, hex) to <fpr>.

Exactly one ticket directory, with exactly one root event. Every parent an event names is present in the same directory, so the Merkle DAG the log commits to is complete.

The pinned definition travels. The create event carries :ticket/process-hash, and processes/by-hash/<that hash>.edn holds the definition whose content address equals it.

identity/ holds excerpts. A key binding travels as the single registry event that made it, with its own authorship signature and the issuer’s public key. Its parents live in a registry ticket that stays behind, so its standing rests on its content address plus the issuer’s signature over the id-token it carries.

Delegations travel with the verdicts they cover. A verdict signed by the throwaway key of a tik review --batch (ADR 0037) counts only through the delegation that names the key, so the bundle carries every delegation covering one of its events, and delegation.edn ({:require-touch true} or false) when the store sets a delegation policy. A bundle without delegation.edn credits delegations without a touch requirement, as a store without a policy does.

The role register travels where the store keeps one. roles.edn maps each role to its members in the shape a definition declares, {:role {:members ["actor" …]} …}, and replaces the definition’s members role by role. A bundle without roles.edn re-derives under the definition’s members, as a store without a register does. A roles.edn that is present and does not parse, does not have that shape, or is not a regular file makes the bundle unreadable: a reader refuses it rather than fall back to the definition’s members, because the register is how a member’s departure is expressed. The file carries no content address and no signature, so it states the membership the producing store held without proving it.

bundle.edn declares the packaging version and nothing else. The ticket, the head, the definition and the stage are derivable from the files, so the manifest names none of them and nothing in it is trusted. A bundle without a manifest is version 1.

The checks

These are what the format promises. verify.sh implements them with coreutils, ssh-keygen and — for key bindings — openssl; tik rederive implements them in process. The script travels inside the archive it checks, so read it before you run it, or run this list yourself.

  1. Integrity. Every tickets/*/events/*.edn, identity/*.edn, processes/by-hash/*.edn and tickets/*/blobs/* hashes to its own name.
  2. Shape. Exactly one ticket directory.
  3. Completeness. Every parent referenced by an event is present, and exactly one event has empty :event/parents.
  4. Authorship. Every .sig. sidecar verifies as the actor its own event names — binding -I to :event/actor rather than accepting whoever happened to sign, so a registered actor cannot sign another’s authorship. Every .pqsig. sidecar likewise verifies as its event’s actor through a pq-signers line that allows the tik-event namespace. A .pqsig. sidecar without pq-signers fails, and verify.sh fails one it cannot check because the host’s OpenSSL is older than 3.5. A .sig. sidecar whose key actors does not grant still counts when a delegation in identity/ covers it:
    • the delegation is an attestation by the event’s actor, verifying through an actors line no key binding earned, and touched where delegation.edn requires it;
    • its window is at most five minutes and holds the event’s :event/at;
    • its scope names the event’s ticket together with one of the event’s parents;
    • its facts name the path the event asserts;
    • the sidecar verifies against the key the delegation names.
  5. Countersignature. Every .witness. sidecar verifies as a registered principal under tik-witness. Every .pqwitness. sidecar is an ML-DSA-65 signature over tik-witness-v1\0 followed by the event’s bytes, by a pq-signers key allowed tik-witness.
  6. Signature policy. Where signatures.edn travels, it reads as {:require #{:ssh-ed25519 …} :from <instant>} over the algorithms :ssh-ed25519 and :ml-dsa-65, or the bundle fails. Every event carries a verifying ssh-ed25519 signature by its actor; from :from on, also one for every other required algorithm; and where :ml-dsa-65 is required, every event claimed before :from is a .pqwitness. event or one of its ancestors.
  7. Key bindings. For each binding in identity/: the issuer signed the id-token, using the key at identity/keys/<kid>.pem; the token’s sub and iss equal the binding’s; the token was live at the binding’s :event/at; the token names the key it binds, as a nonce or an aud suffix equal to tik-key-<sha256 of the key> (ADR 0035); and the key it binds appears in actors.

Check 7 is checkable offline because the issuer’s key travels in the archive, and it says exactly this much: whoever built this bundle holds a token that this key signed, for this subject and this bound key, at that moment. Recognizing the key as the issuer’s is the reader’s job, the same way recognizing an actors line is — a subject like repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main is worth what the reader knows about that repository and that IdP.

An unsigned event is authenticity unclaimed rather than a failure, and a binding whose issuer key is absent grants nothing and is reported as such. Everything else in the list is a failure.

Deriving the ticket’s stages needs the definition as well, which is where tik rederive goes on and verify.sh stops.

Compatibility

Version 1 is the layout above. The rules below are what a reader written against it may rely on.

A reader ignores what it does not recognize. Unknown files, directories and manifest keys are passed over. That is what makes the additions in the next paragraph safe.

These may appear without a version bump:

  • new top-level files and directories;
  • new files inside existing directories, including new sidecar kinds (<id>.<kind>.<fingerprint>);
  • new keys in bundle.edn;
  • new event types, fact paths, guard operators and process keys inside the files, which are versioned by the kernel’s own vocabularies rather than by this format;
  • any change to verify.sh and README.md, which carry no contract of their own.

These force a version bump:

  • moving, renaming or removing anything the layout names;
  • changing what a name means — a different hash function, a different suffix convention, a signature namespace;
  • changing the canonical serialization, which changes every event id and is versioned separately by tik.canonical/format-version;
  • carrying more than one ticket;
  • anything else that makes a conforming version-1 reader compute a different answer or fail.

A reader holding a bundle whose major version it does not know declines it and says so.

Reading a bundle yourself

The archive unpacks to plain files, so an implementation in any language is a hash, a signature check and an EDN reader.

mkdir bundle && tar xzf evidence.tgz -C bundle && cd bundle

# 1. integrity, without any tool of ours
sha256sum tickets/*/events/*.edn | while read sum f; do
  [ "sha256-$sum" = "$(basename "$f" .edn)" ] || echo "MISMATCH $f"
done

# 2. authorship, as the actor each event names
for sig in tickets/*/events/*.sig.*; do
  ev="${sig%%.sig.*}.edn"
  actor=$(sed -n 's/^{:event\/actor "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$ev")
  ssh-keygen -Y verify -f actors -I "$actor" -n tik-event -s "$sig" < "$ev"
done

Canonical bytes sort map keys, so :event/actor always leads an event file — which is why one sed finds it.

Relationship to in-toto

in-toto attestations describe a build: this subject, this predicate, signed by this functionary. A bundle carries a different kind of thing — the facts, the rules that judge them, and the means to recompute the verdict offline. in-toto’s nearest analogue is the layout, and a tik process definition already is one.

The two compose. tik bridge intoto reads a SLSA provenance, an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM, or a vulnerability report into an attestation event, so an :attested-within guard is satisfied by the format your pipeline already emits, and the result travels in a bundle.

entry.title: Clojure library
entry.content:
Read, verify and derive one ticket of a store in process with tik.api, read-only and without starting a process.

tik.api gives a JVM, babashka or native-image program the answers of tik status and tik verify for one ticket without running the CLI. It never writes to the store, signs, runs a probe, touches the network or starts a process.

(require '[tik.api :as api])

(def store (api/open-store "/path/to/.tik"))   ; the dir holding tickets/ or tik.db

(api/derive store "f106aa78")
;; => {:ticket #uuid "f106aa78-…" :title "…"
;;     :rules {:process :skilled-change :version 2 :hash "sha256-…"}
;;     :current [:scoped] :reached [:scoped]
;;     :facts {[:kind] {:status :present :value :feat :by "claude"} …}
;;     :missing-parents nil
;;     :definition {:pinned "sha256-…" :derived-under "sha256-…" :source :archive}
;;     :at #inst "…"}

(:ok? (api/verify-ticket store "f106aa78"))

Add tik as a git dependency in deps.edn:

{:deps {io.github.metio/tik {:git/sha "<commit>"}}}

The calls

  • (open-store root) or (open-store root {:limits {…}}) opens the store whose root is root, the directory holding tickets/ (file store) or tik.db (SQLite store). Nothing is discovered from parent directories.
  • (resolve-id store ref) takes a uuid, the full id, or a prefix of at least 8 characters naming exactly one ticket.
  • (ticket store ref) returns the ticket’s events in reduction order.
  • (derive store ref {:at instant}) returns the ticket’s title, rules, current and reached stages and facts. They equal what tik status <id> --edn --at <instant> prints. When the definition found in the store does not hash to the ticket’s pin, derive refuses unless {:allow-unpinned-definition true} is passed.
  • (verify-ticket store ref) runs the tik verify ladder for that ticket with the same code as the CLI and returns it as data: :ok?, :failures, one summary per event (:integrity and :signature, which is :verified, :delegated, :unsigned, :unchecked or :failed) and every check as an item.

tik.api/version is the contract’s version; it changes only when a documented key, argument or refusal changes meaning or goes away.

Refusals

Every refusal is an ex-info whose :type is in the tik.api namespace: not-a-store, ambiguous-store, backend-unavailable, invalid-argument, invalid-id, unknown-ticket, ambiguous-id (with :candidates), too-large (with :limit and :actual), unreadable, definition-missing, definition-mismatch, malformed-roles, underivable and read-only.

Differences from the CLI

  • Signatures are verified in process (Ed25519, Ed25519 security keys, ML-DSA-65). A key type only ssh-keygen reads is :unchecked, and its check fails where tik verify would ask ssh-keygen.
  • Every event, sidecar and config file is measured before it is read, and a symbolic link inside a ticket directory is refused. The defaults are tik.api/default-limits.
  • A SQLite store is opened read-only and needs the SQLite driver, which babashka lacks. A native image that reads SQLite stores or identity bindings must require tik.store.sqlite-jdbc or cheshire.core at build time.

The reasoning is recorded in ADR 0044 .

entry.title: Evidence
entry.content:
The published bundle format, and how anyone re-derives what a bundle’s facts imply under the rules it pinned.

A ticket travels as an evidence bundle: the signed facts, the hash-pinned rules that judge them, the registry the signatures check against, and a script that checks the lot with coreutils. Whoever holds one recomputes the answer.

That is the whole claim, and it is a narrow one. A build system tells you a process ran. A bundle tells you which rules judged it, what they required, what was supplied, and lets you recompute the verdict on a laptop with no network, years later.

  • Bundle format — the on-disk contract, what a reader may assume, and what forces a version bump.
  • Re-deriving a bundle — tik rederive, the HTTP service, and what a badge is allowed to say.
  • SLSA, said honestly — what the release processes demand, mapped onto SLSA’s requirements, and where that mapping stops.

What a bundle is worth

A guard checks that a trusted attester said something. It never reads the SBOM. So a derivation is exactly as good as the attesters named in it, and that belongs in the first paragraph rather than a footnote — the signatures prove who claimed, the hashes prove what was claimed, and the definition proves which rule accepted it.

What the format adds on top of a signed archive is the rules. Two people holding the same bundle reach the same stages, because the definition that judged the ticket travels inside it, addressed by its own hash.

entry.title: Machine-checked proofs
entry.content:
What a Lean 4 model of the derivation function proves about stages, what it leaves out, and how CI holds the model and the Clojure kernel to the same answers.

Three laws of derivation are proved in Lean 4 over an executable model of tik.stage/reached-set, evolve and effective-reached, and CI runs that model beside the Clojure kernel on every pull request and fails on any disagreement. The proofs say nothing about the Clojure code directly; the differential run is what ties the two together, case by case.

What is proved

The model and its proofs live in formal/lean/. Every theorem below rests on Lean’s three standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) and nothing else; bb lean fails on a sorry, an added axiom or native_decide anywhere in a proof.

  • Event order. Two lists holding the same events, in any order and with any duplicates, derive the same stages, sticky carry included (Tik.derive_order_independent). The one assumption is the content-addressing promise: two events with the same id are the same event.
  • Sweep order. Listing a definition’s stages in another order derives the same reached set, for any facts and any sticky carry, as long as stage ids are distinct (Tik.reachedSet_perm).
  • One fixpoint. For a stratified process, exactly one set of stages is closed under the rules (a stage is in it exactly when its :after stages are and its guards hold reading it), and the synchronous sweep from an empty carry computes that set (Tik.stratified_unique_fixpoint).
  • Monotonicity. Adding facts, keeping every fact already present with its value and author, never removes a stage whose guards, and the guards of every stage it waits for, contain no :not (Tik.reachedSet_mono_cone).

Stratified here means ADR 0033’s rule in certificate form: every stage a stage waits for, through :after or a positive [:stage-reached …], has a smaller entry bound, and every stage it negates enters for good before the stage is first judged. The model checks the certificate for every case it runs; every process in processes/ passes it.

Counterexamples

Each stronger statement below is false, and the model proves so on a concrete process:

  • Firing one stage at a time reaches two different terminal sets on processes/sweep-order.edn, depending on the order; the synchronous sweep reaches one.
  • Two stages that wait for each other through positive [:stage-reached …] guards have two fixpoints, the empty set and both stages. The lint accepts such a pair, since nothing negates either stage; the sweep derives the empty one.
  • A stage with no guard at all drops out when a fact arrives that a stage it waits for negates. Monotonicity therefore needs every stage upstream to be free of :not too.
  • A later assertion that changes a fact’s value can remove a stage gated by :fact=. Adding an event is adding a fact only when the event names a path that held no value.

What is left out

The model’s guard basis is :fact, :fact=, :signed-by, :different-person, :stage-reached, :and, :or and :not. Its reduction knows assertions and retractions, last write wins in (at, id) order. Left out, each because its verdict is fixed for one evaluation of the fixpoint and adds nothing to the laws above:

  • :artifact, :elapsed-since, :attested-within and :malli, and the schemas a definition declares for its facts. The kernel computes these and hands the model the verdicts.
  • disputes, conflicts between concurrent writes and the :now clamp, which the reducer resolves before guards run;
  • signatures, key bindings and the role register, which decide which events and members exist, before derivation starts.

The fixpoint and monotonicity theorems are stated for an empty sticky carry. With a carry, derivation depends on the history it was carried through, and the differential run covers it.

The differential run

bb lean builds the model, checks the axioms, replays the proofs with leanchecker, and then derives every case twice: once with tik.stage, once with the model’s executable tik-lean. The cases are the conformance corpus, every scripted case under processes/*.tests.edn and a few thousand generated processes and histories, lint-clean or not. A case whose guards and events fit the model is replayed from its events; any other case gets the kernel’s facts and sticky carry, with every guard outside the basis replaced by its verdict.

bb lean controls shows that each check can fail: a planted sorry must fail the source check and the axiom check, and four deliberately broken models (firing one stage per sweep, seeding the carry into the first snapshot, ignoring :after, ignoring retractions) must each disagree with the kernel on some case.

Toolchain

The Lean release is pinned in formal/lean/lean-toolchain and installed by breto for the CI job; bb lean refuses a lean on PATH of any other version. The model uses Lean’s core library only, without Mathlib or Batteries.

entry.title: Re-deriving a bundle
entry.content:
tik rederive checks a bundle and recomputes what its facts imply — at a terminal, or over HTTP with a badge that names the derivation.

verify.sh answers one question: are these bytes what they claim to be? tik rederive answers the other one: what do they add up to?

tik rederive evidence.tgz

bundle sha256-04a0bf413895fefb1c20e9231632fbc0d0a0d768275b42c097581ed19365973a
  format    tik-evidence-bundle version 1
  ticket    e26a1d57-6643-4564-99fa-8968ced7afa5  "2026.8.6132954"
  events    10
  judged by release sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca

verification
  ok   … hashes to its name and is schema-valid
  ok   every referenced parent is present
  ok   exactly one root event
  ok   … verifies as ci
  ok   ci is bound to its key by repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main, per …
  => the bytes are what they claim to be

derivation at 2026-08-06T20:29:26.198Z
  reached   :attested, :built, :scanned
  current   :attested, :scanned
  :built
      ✓ [:fact [:version]]
      ✓ [:signed-by :ci [:commit]]
      ✓ [:artifact "checksums/"]
  :scanned
      ✓ [:attested-within :vulnerability-scan "P1D"]

It takes a .tgz, an unpacked directory, or an https URL, and exits 1 when the bundle fails to verify — a derivation over bytes that are not what they claim to be is worth nothing. --edn prints the same result as data.

A bundle whose roles.edn is present but does not read as a role register is refused with exit 1 and nothing derived from it; the service answers such a bundle with status 400. Without roles.edn, the definition’s members stand (see Bundle format ).

Derivation names its instant

reached above is what the pinned rules grant at the instant printed under it. The release process demands a vulnerability scan attested within a day; a month from now the same archive, byte for byte, derives :built alone — the scan it carries is real, signed, and too old for the rule that reads it.

That is the reason to re-derive rather than record. A stored “passed” survives its own evidence; a derivation ages with it.

Gating on a bundle

Three flags turn re-derivation into a check a consumer’s own CI can stand on:

tik rederive https://example.com/evidence.tgz \
  --expect-stage :published \
  --expect-definition sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca

Exit 0 when every named stage is reached under that exact definition, 1 otherwise, with a line saying which expectation failed and what was derived instead.

Pin the definition. A bundle carries the rules that judged it, so a supplier who writes those rules can reach any stage they choose — :published becomes a claim about a process only once the reader names which process. That is why --expect-definition takes the full hash and refuses an abbreviation: eight hex characters is thirty-two bits for somebody to collide with deliberately, and the value is pasted into a workflow file once.

Name who may bind a key. A key the bundle earned through an identity binding was accepted under the supplier’s binding policy and checked against issuer keys the supplier shipped, and the supplier chose both. A token signed by a key the supplier made up can name any issuer and subject. --expect-bindings applies your policy and your keys instead. The policy has the shape oidc.edn uses:

{:bindings {"ci" [{:issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
                   :subject "repo:supplier/proj:ref:refs/heads/main"}]}}

tik rederive evidence.tgz --expect-bindings reader-oidc.edn

The issuer keys are read from jwks/ beside that file, the layout a tik store root already has, so a reader who runs tik points at their own oidc.edn and pins issuers with tik bridge jwks. Every bound key must then come from an issuer and subject your file permits for that actor, with a token a key you pinned for that issuer signed. A subject ending in * admits every subject that starts with what precedes it. A bundle whose signers are all listed in its actors file passes and says that no signer rests on a binding. A file without :bindings, or one that does not parse, is refused: a policy that says nothing would pass every bundle.

In GitHub Actions

permissions:
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/install@2026.8.7062815
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/verify@2026.8.7062815
    with:
      bundle: https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz
      expect-stage: ":published"
      expect-definition: "sha256-3c577f36…"

The ref you pin is the tik you get: with no version input, the installer resolves the release matching its own ref, so a pinned action and a pinned tool are one decision rather than two.

The installer verifies before it trusts. It fetches the release’s SHA256SUMS, checks the cosign keyless signature naming the release workflow that produced it, and only then checks the binary against those checksums — an installer for a verification tool has no business asking you to trust an unverified download. Linux/amd64 gets the native binary; other platforms get the portable jar and need a JDK already on PATH.

verify needs tik on PATH and does one thing with it, so bring your own build if you have one.

The service

tik rederive --serve --port 7788

POST /rederive                     the bundle as the request body -> EDN
GET  /derivation?bundle=<url>      fetch it, re-derive, render the page
GET  /badge.svg?bundle=<url>       the same, as a badge

Every request re-derives. The one thing held between requests is a cache keyed by the bundle’s content address and the minute the answer was computed for — both inputs to the derivation, both immutable, so an entry is either exactly right or absent and the whole cache is disposable.

The service fetches https URLs whose every resolved address is public, follows at most four redirects, checking each hop, and caps what it will download. It runs nothing from inside a bundle: the verify.sh that travels in an archive is a convenience for whoever chooses to run it, and the service implements the checks itself.

Point a README badge at a release artifact:

[![evidence](https://your-host/badge.svg?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)](https://your-host/derivation?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)

What a badge says

The stages the pinned definition grants, and which definition granted them: release@3c577f36 · :attested · :scanned. The badge links to a page carrying the guards that held, the ones that did not, who may sign in this bundle and on whose say-so, and the two commands that reach the same answer with the service switched off.

A badge is a derived conclusion displayed as though it were a fact, which is the one thing derived beats declared forbids storing. Three properties keep it honest:

  • it is derived per request, so it is a lens rather than a status;
  • it names the derivation — stages, definition hash, instant — where a word like compliant would name a policy it cannot see;
  • the service is disposable. Delete it and the bundle still checks out with coreutils. A verification service that becomes the authority has re-introduced exactly the trust the bundle removes.

The colour follows the same rule: one shade for a bundle that verifies, red for one that does not. Green would read as approval, and the badge reports a derivation, which is a different kind of claim.

Publishing bundles from CI

The wedge is one line over evidence a pipeline already produces. tik’s own release workflow records the version, the commit, the image digest and the checksums file as signed facts, imports the SBOM, provenance and scan as attestations through tik bridge intoto, and ships the result:

tik bundle "$TICKET" --out "evidence-$VERSION.tgz"

CI signs with an ephemeral key bound to its workload identity (ADR 0023 ), so the bundle carries the binding and its issuer’s key, and a recipient re-earns that trust from the issuer’s own signature.
